Organizations pursuing lower cost per hire tend to lean on four strategies with recurring evidence behind them: employee referral programs, recruitment automation and ATS tools, employer branding, and internal mobility. The data on effectiveness is strongest for the first three; internal promotion is discussed often but rarely quantified in the same way.

**Employee referral programs** carry the most consistent savings figures across sources. Jobvite research cited by ATS+Partners puts the reduction in cost per hire from referrals at up to 50%, attributed to faster processing and less need for advertising or agency fees [4]. LinkedIn data in the same piece found referred employees have a 45% higher retention rate than hires from other channels, and a Zipdo report found referred candidates get hired 55% faster [4]. A 2024 study by the referral platform ERIN, based on over 1.1 million referrals from more than 744,000 users, found that roughly 1 in 10 referrals converts to a hire at enterprise organizations, compared with the 50-60 applicants companies typically need per hire through job boards [6]. That study also broke down the funnel: of 10 candidates who receive a referral notice, eight respond, six apply, four interview, and one gets hired [6]. Real company examples back this up: at JLL, over 11,000 referrals from more than 13,500 employees produced over 600 offers [6], and at SHRM, about 50% of referrals became hires, with referrals making up slightly more than 10% of all hires in 2024 [6]. Deloitte's structured referral program produced a 25% reduction in hiring costs, and referred candidates there were 40% more likely to stay beyond three years [9]. Referral bonuses in practice range from a $25 gift card up to $1,000 or more depending on role difficulty [6], with one pricing guide citing a typical range of $500 to $2,000 [9]. One caveat raised by SHRM's director of talent acquisition: referrals can carry baked-in bias if hiring managers give referred candidates less scrutiny than other applicants, so structured programs still need consistent interview processes [6].

**Recruitment automation and ATS tools** show the widest range of cited savings, largely because the underlying research comes from vendors with product-specific case studies rather than independent academic study. A commonly cited range is 20-40% lower cost per hire from AI screening and scheduling, with average savings around 33% in both time-to-hire and cost-per-hire, and enterprise companies reportedly saving $2.3 million annually [1]. PwC is cited for a figure of 340% average ROI within 18 months for AI recruitment tools, and SHRM is cited for 31% faster hiring and a 50% improvement in quality-of-hire metrics among companies using AI-powered recruitment tools [1]. A separate analysis attributed to Cadient's client data found that companies tracking a full set of hiring metrics (time to hire, cost per hire, applicant conversion, quality of hire, recruiter productivity, retention rate) saw 43% faster hiring and 32% lower turnover than companies that didn't [2]. One ATS-focused source put a specific before/after: cost-per-hire falling from $3,500 to $1,900 (nearly half), agency reliance dropping from 50% to 25%, cost-per-qualified-applicant falling from $120 to $70, admin hours per hire dropping from 8-12 to 3-6, and time-to-hire shortening from 40 to 26 days [3]. A DemandSage analysis cited elsewhere found organizations using AI recruiting tools report cost-per-hire reductions of 30% or more and 300-500% ROI within the first year [5]. More targeted automation examples include video interviewing, said to reduce cost per hire by around 20% [7], and Unilever's adoption of the AI video interview platform HireVue, which reduced screening time by 75% and lowered cost per hire by $6,000 for graduate roles, producing more than $1 million in annual global savings [9].

**Employer branding** also has specific figures attached, though again mostly from single-company case studies rather than broad surveys. A LinkedIn study is cited for finding that companies with strong employer brands have up to 43% lower cost per hire [7]. A branded career portal is said to attract up to 8 times more direct applicants than relying on job boards alone [7]. Individual company examples: Ericsson cut its cost per hire by 70% through social media and employee advocacy initiatives [7]; Nokia reduced cost per hire by 74% by switching its primary posting platform to Indeed [7]; HubSpot's "Culture Code" video and transparent Glassdoor presence saved over $10,000 per recruiting campaign by reducing reliance on paid ads [9]; Canva's "Life at Canva" content increased inbound applications by 60% and let the company cut paid recruitment ads, saving over $50,000 annually [9]; and Zapier, by avoiding paid job boards in favor of organic LinkedIn posts and niche boards like We Work Remotely, saved over $30,000 annually while maintaining a steady flow of qualified applicants [9].

**Internal promotion and mobility** is recommended consistently as a cost-reduction lever, on the logic that it avoids external advertising and agency fees and leads to faster integration, but the sources available here do not attach a specific percentage savings figure to it the way they do for referrals, automation, or branding [7]. That gap is worth noting directly if the Wikipedia entry compares strategies by effect size, since it means internal mobility is qualitatively supported but not quantified in this set of sources.

Time-to-Fill FAQs What are time-to-fill metrics? Time-to-fill measures the number of days between when a job requisition is opened and when an offer is accepted (or, in some organizations, when the new hire starts). It’s one of the most widely tracked recruiting metrics because it reflects both the efficiency of the hiring process and the organization’s ability to compete for talent. What’s time-to-fill versus time-to-hire? These terms are often confused but measure slightly different things: - Time-to-fill → From the date a requisition is opened until an offer is accepted (sometim
[6]: es tracked until the start date). - Time-to-hire → From the date a candidate enters the pipeline (e.g., applies or is sourced) until the day they accept the offer. In short, time-to-fill reflects the organization’s overall hiring speed, while time-to-hire reflects the candidate’s journey once in the funnel. What’s the average time-to-fill? It varies widely by role and industry. HR.com’s Future of Recruitment Technologies report found: - Entry-level roles: 30–60 days (with a quarter taking 90+ days). - Mid-level roles: 31–60 days for most, 17% stretching past 90. - Senior roles: Nearly 40% take longer than 90 days. - Nonexempt roles: Typically 30–60 days, though 25% still exceed 90. External benchmarks place the U.S. average at ~35 days, slightly faster than the global average of 38.

HR sources are fairly consistent on the core distinction but diverge on some details, and there is real, cited data on where delays pile up inside the hiring window.

## The core distinction

Most sources define **time-to-hire** as the candidate-facing metric: the clock starts when a candidate enters the pipeline (applies or is sourced) and stops when that same candidate accepts the offer [1][2][3][5][7][8][9]. It measures how efficiently the organization moves one candidate through screening, interviews, and negotiation once they're already in the funnel [9].

**Time-to-fill** is the broader, organization-facing metric. It starts earlier, usually at job requisition approval, submission, or posting, and ends at the same point (offer acceptance, sometimes extended to the candidate's start date) [1][2][3][5][6][8]. Because it includes everything before a candidate even shows up (approvals, job description drafting, sourcing, advertising), it's consistently the longer of the two numbers [1][3][5].

AIHR frames the difference this way: time-to-hire is "candidate-centered" and useful for optimizing the recruitment process a candidate experiences, while time-to-fill "gives you an overview of the speed and quality of your entire recruitment process" and supports business planning [3]. HeartCount puts it more bluntly: time-to-fill is a planning and resource metric that reflects internal control (approvals, recruiter bandwidth, cross-department coordination), while time-to-hire is an execution metric that reflects the candidate's experience of the funnel once they're in it [5].

## Where the start point actually varies

The one place sources disagree, and several flag this explicitly, is exactly where time-to-fill's clock starts. Documented options include:

- Job requisition submitted by the hiring manager, before approval [1][2]
- Job requisition approved [3][5][6]
- Job posting goes live/advertised [1][2][7][8]

Indeed and AIHR both note this isn't a settled industry standard; AIHR's guidance is simply "be consistent in your tracking" so results are comparable across roles and over time, since inconsistent start points make benchmarking meaningless [2][3]. The end point has the same ambiguity: some organizations stop the clock at offer acceptance, others extend it to the new hire's first day [2][3][6].

## The formulas as documented

Time-to-hire:
Time to Hire = Date of offer acceptance − Date of application (or sourcing) [5][9]
Example given: applied January 1, accepted February 1 → 31 days [9]. A second worked example: applied day 4 of a posting, offer accepted day 10 → 6 days [2].

Time-to-fill:
Time to Fill = Date of offer acceptance − Date requisition approved/posted [3][5]
Example given: requisition opened March 1, candidate accepted March 25 → 24 days [5]. Averages are computed by summing the days-to-fill across all roles closed in a period and dividing by the number of roles [1][2][3].

## Documented benchmarks

Reported averages cluster in a fairly narrow band but vary by source and year:

| Metric | Reported average | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Time-to-hire (overall) | ~44 days | [1][5][7] |
| Time-to-fill (overall) | ~44 days | [1][7] |
| Time-to-fill (SHRM, 2024) | ~54 days | [5] |
| Time-to-fill, US average | 43 days | Workable study, cited in [3] |
| Time-to-fill, UK & Ireland | 48 days | Workable study, cited in [3] |
| Time-to-fill, US (2025, external benchmark) | ~35 days | [6] |
| Time-to-fill, engineering roles | 58 days (US/UK), 56 (rest of Europe/world) | Workable study, cited in [3] |
| Time-to-fill, healthcare | 29 days | Workable study, cited in [3] |

## Data on where the delay accumulates

This is where the sourcing gets more concrete. HR.com's Future of Recruitment Technologies 2025-26 report, cited by Mitratech, breaks time-to-fill down by role level rather than by process stage, and the spread is wide [6]:

- Entry-level roles: most organizations report 30 to 60 days, with a quarter taking 90+ days
- Mid-level roles: 44% report 31 to 60 days, 17% exceed 90 days
- Senior-level roles: nearly 40% take more than 90 days
- Exempt roles: 44% fall in the 31-60 day window, almost 40% exceed 90
- Nonexempt roles: mostly 30 to 60 days, but 25% still exceed 90

The same report attributes the delays in mid-level and nonexempt roles, which "should" move faster, to internal friction rather than market scarcity: approval bottlenecks, outdated systems, and manual handoffs that consume recruiter hours, compounded by multi-jurisdiction compliance requirements and expanding background-check rules [6].

Several sources point to specific stages as the recurring bottlenecks:

- **Approvals and sign-off.** AIHR lists "resolving inefficiencies" as a direct benefit of tracking time-to-fill, since it exposes which roles and departments take longest, often traced to requisition and approval cycles [3]. HeartCount states plainly that "a long requisition approval process can extend time-to-fill even if the hiring team moves quickly after sourcing" [5]. Indeed's HR data lists "slow approvals" among the common factors that delay hiring [1].
- **Interview scheduling.** AIHR cites a study finding that 62% of senior candidates have left a recruitment process specifically because of scheduling delays [3]. Mitratech reports that scheduling automation (removing "calendar ping-pong") saves 4 to 8+ days per hire, based on client data from Mitratech's own vendor, Mitratech [6].
- **Sourcing and candidate response.** AIHR cites data showing 23% of candidates lose interest if they don't hear back within one week, rising to 46% within one to two weeks [3]. Appcast's application-rate data, cited by Mitratech, shows apply rates spike as friction drops: from 3.6% of visitors completing an application when it takes 15+ minutes, up to 12.5% when it takes under five minutes [6].
- **Offer negotiation and acceptance.** SmartRecruiters data, cited by Mitratech, puts the US offer-acceptance rate at 79%, described as the lowest among peer markets, meaning even organizations with fast time-to-fill are still losing candidates at the final stage [6].
- **Technology gaps.** Mitratech reports that while 70%+ of organizations use an applicant tracking system, fewer than half use automated interview scheduling, onboarding automation, or recruitment analytics, leaving recruiters doing manually what tooling could otherwise absorb [6].

## What isn't in the gathered sources

None of the material provided gives a single, unified stage-by-stage time breakdown for one process (for example, "X days average in sourcing, Y days in approvals, Z days in interviewing, W days in offer negotiation" for the same cohort of hires). The closest is HR.com's breakdown by role seniority [6] and the scattered stage-specific figures above (scheduling costing 4-8+ days, candidates dropping off after 1-2 weeks of silence, offer-acceptance rates). A Wikipedia article on this topic would need to present these as separate, source-specific data points rather than pieces of one consistent funnel breakdown, since the underlying studies (Workable, SHRM, HR.com/Mitratech, Appcast, SmartRecruiters) measured different things on different populations.

The standard cost-per-hire figure that most companies report is a straightforward average built from recruiting and onboarding expenses divided by the number of hires made. The Society for Human Resource Management (SHRM) puts this baseline at roughly $4,700 per hire for non-executive roles, a number that has risen about 14% since pre-pandemic levels, and closer to $28,000 to $28,329 when the hire is an executive [2][5][7]. The formula behind it is Total Cost-Per-Hire = (External Costs + Internal Costs) ÷ Number of Hires, where external costs include job board fees, recruiter commissions, and background checks, and internal costs include HR and hiring-manager time, interview hours, and administrative processing [1][4][8].

When economists and HR researchers instead calculate the "true cost" of a specific bad hire, they abandon that flat average and switch to a percentage-of-salary or multiple-of-salary model, because a mis-hire's damage scales with seniority rather than staying fixed. The U.S. Department of Labor sets the conservative floor at 30% of the employee's first-year earnings, but this figure is explicitly limited to direct replacement costs and does not include productivity loss, management drain, or cultural impact [1][2][3][5][7][9]. SHRM's broader range runs from 50% to 200% of annual salary, sliding from about 50 to 75% for entry-level roles up to 200% or more for C-suite positions [1][2][7]. Other researchers cite different multiples for the same phenomenon: Robert Half puts the figure at 15 to 21% of annual salary [3], PwC and the Recruitment & Employment Confederation estimate 50 to 150% once compensation, training, HR expenses, and lost productivity are factored in [6], and Oxford Economics found the cost can reach 120% of salary in certain sectors [6]. CareerBuilder reports a flat average loss of about $17,000 per bad hire, climbing to $240,000 or more for specialized or executive positions [2][7], and one analysis frames the full organizational impact of a senior or strategic bad hire at three to five times annual salary, meaning a $150,000 role can carry a true cost of $450,000 to $750,000 [9].

The gap between the two figures comes from the components the "true cost" calculation adds on top of the visible recruiting and salary spend. These typically include:

- Lost productivity and ramp-up time, since a new hire can take three to twelve months to reach full output, and Gallup data shows disengaged employees cost businesses $3,400 for every $10,000 in salary [1][2].
- Management and leadership time drain: Harvard Business Review found managers spend about 17% more time supervising a poor performer than a solid one, and one source estimates 10 to 15 hours per week of unplanned leadership attention for a director-level bad hire, or 260 to 390 hours over six months [2][9].
- Team productivity decline, with one estimate putting the drag on a high-performing team at 15 to 25% when one member is misaligned [9].
- Training investment that is lost when the employee leaves, averaging around $1,300 per employee per year in the U.S. [2].
- Cultural and morale costs, including disengagement (Gallup estimates disengaged employees cost the U.S. economy $450 to $550 billion annually, or the global economy $8.8 trillion, about 9% of world GDP) and cascading turnover, since 54% of employees report leaving a job because of poor workplace culture [1][5].
- Customer and revenue impact, since roughly 32% of customers stop doing business with a company after one bad experience [5].
- Opportunity cost from missed performance, illustrated by the example of a VP of Operations who should be driving $2 million in efficiency gains but delivers none, a shortfall that is itself counted as part of the bad hire's cost [9].
- Reputational damage and, in severe cases, fraud or misconduct risk [6].

Because DOL's 30% figure is described by its own source as covering only "the conservative floor of direct replacement costs," and because SHRM's percentage range and the other estimates above are built specifically to fold in these indirect categories, the "true cost" of a bad hire is consistently reported as several multiples higher than the standard cost-per-hire average companies track for routine reporting [1][2][7][9].

The gap between the two figures comes from the components the "true cost" calculation adds on top of the visible recruiting and salary spend. These typically include:

- Lost productivity and ramp-up time, since a new hire can take three to twelve months to reach full output, and Gallup data shows disengaged employees cost businesses $3,400 for every $10,000 in salary [1][2].

- Training investment that is lost when the employee leaves, averaging around $1,300 per employee per year in the U.S. [2].
- Cultural and morale costs, including disengagement (Gallup estimates disengaged employees cost the U.S. economy $450 to $550 billion annually, or the global economy $8.8 trillion, about 9% of world GDP) and cascading turnover, since 54% of employees report leaving a job because of poor workplace culture [1][5].
- Customer and revenue impact, since roughly 32% of customers stop doing business with a company after one bad experience [5].
- Opportunity cost from missed performance, illustrated by the example of a VP of Operations who should be driving $2 million in efficiency gains but delivers none, a shortfall that is itself counted as part of the bad hire's cost [9].
- Reputational damage and, in severe cases, fraud or misconduct risk [6].

Because DOL's 30% figure is described by its own source as covering only "the conservative floor of direct replacement costs," and because SHRM's percentage range and the other estimates above are built specifically to fold in these indirect categories, the "true cost" of a bad hire is consistently reported as several multiples higher than the standard cost-per-hire average companies track for routine reporting [1][2][7][9].

Involuntary termination is when a company removes an employee from their post and thus ends the employment relationship. This can happen due to poor performance, unprofessional behavior, or a strategic shift within the company. It differs from voluntary termination and mutual termination in that the employee has no say in the decision. There are two types of involuntary termination — with cause and without cause. With Cause “With Cause” termination is when a company fires an employee for a reason. These reasons include poor performance, a violation of company policy, repeated lateness, or violence/aggressive behavior in the workplace. In most cases, the company will have warned the employee that they face dismissal if they do not change their performance/behavior. In many instances, businesses may have offered a performance improvement plan to struggling employees. However, there are instances when a company will fire an employee without prior warning. For example, if an employee threatens others in the
[4]: workplace or otherwise grossly violates company policy. Without Cause Involuntary termination doesn’t always mean that the employee has done something wrong. In some cases, a company will remove an employee from their post through no fault of the employee. This is “without cause.” For instance, if a company runs into financial difficulties or downsizes and has to lay-off staff. This type of termination relates to a company’s business objectives or wider economic conditions. How to calculate the turnover rate Involuntary termination is more than an incidental employment factor. It’s in the company’s best interests to keep the turnover rate low, both for voluntary and involuntary termination. As such, HR should measure the employee turnover rate as a key performance indicator (KPI). If it’s too high, there could be an issue with employee engagement, management performance, or the broader company culture. A high employee attrition rate can result in lost productivity and increased employee costs. There are ways to improve the involuntary termination rate, but first, HR needs to know the rate. So how do you do that? It’s a simple enough formula, providing you have the data you need (an
[4]: d a calculator). You’ll need to know how many involuntary terminations occurred within a set period (of your choosing: the past month, six months, or year are most common). You can find this number by going through the termination documents in your company’s document management software. You’ll also need to know the average number of employees within the same time frame (past month, six months, year). Do this by adding the number of employees at the beginning of the period to the number of employees at the end of the period, then divide by two. For example: The formula for calculating the turnover rate is as follows: To learn the turnover rate for all employees, simply include all staff members that left (voluntary and involuntary). How to Reduce Involuntary Termination Rate There’ll be times when a company has no other choice than to let an employee go. However, if a company has a higher-than-average involuntary termination rate, it’s important to take action. Firing and hiring employees can be highly capital-intensive and result in lost productivity and decreased workplace morale, among other consequences So let’s take a look at some helpful tips that’ll keep the turnover percent
[4]: age to a minimum. Note that these tips only refer to “with cause” terminations, not “without cause” terminations (since those are strategic). Hire Correctly An employee will be more likely to be fired if they were never a good fit in the first place. This isn’t just about their professional capacity to do their task well, though that is important. They should also be in sync with the company’s broader company culture. If they’re not, it’s more likely that problems will arise. Reference checking during the hiring process can also highlight any potential causes for concern. Successful Onboarding Start as you mean to go on, is what they say. If a recruit gets off on the right foot, then they’ll be more likely to succeed in the role. In the case they don’t, then there’ll be a mountain to climb. And mountains are hard to climb. A successful onboarding process will make the employee feel welcome and ensure they can hit the ground running. Ongoing Training Think of hiring the right recruit as planting a seed. The training you provide is the water that nourishes that seed. An unwatered seed will go nowhere. An employee will be more likely to perform well if they’ve got the tools and guidan
[4]: ce to deliver their best work. 70% of employees feel they haven’t mastered the skills they need for their positions. Help employees to feel that they’re learning in their position, and they’ll be better able to contribute to the workplace. Clear Expectations It’s unreasonable to think an employee will follow a company’s guidelines if they don’t know what they are. Your company policy functions to outline appropriate, inappropriate, and unacceptable behavior. This policy should be readily accessible to employees within their employee portal. HR should communicate professional expectations on an individual employee basis via performance appraisals and the employee’s development plan. Offboarding Best Practices It’s a good idea to offboard all employees that leave the company. But it’s extra important when an employee is removed from their post since there’s a greater chance of legal blowbacks. You’ll likely already have your own offboarding process at your business. If you don’t, then download our free offboarding checklist. When dealing with an involuntarily terminated employee, some aspects of offboarding become more critical. For instance, HR should ensure they have all documentat
[4]: ion related to the terminated employee readily available in a document management platform. Revoking access to the company’s platforms and databases is also key. Finally, unless the reason for the dismissal is serious, a farewell is appropriate. This relationship may not have worked out, but what’s done is done. Bid each other well, and move on. Still, it’s an unavoidable part of running a business. While HR teams can’t prevent it entirely, they can use it as a learning opportunity. By diving deep into the data, HR can improve the hiring process, identify employee engagement issues, and ultimately learn from past mistakes.
[5]: As an HR professional, you are aware that there are different types of employee turnover. Your organization is likely losing employees – are they quitting, retiring, or being terminated? And, do you know why? Here are a few employee turnover statistics that may surprise you: - In 2020, the national average annual turnover rate was 57.3% - On average, companies lose 18% of their workforce to turnover each year - In 2018, the overall cost of voluntary employee turnover amounted to $617 billion - Approximately 60-70% of all turnover is voluntary - 33% of employees quit their jobs within the first 90 days of employment - There are over 10 million job openings in the United States - 16.45% of employees quit within their first week of employment, 17.42% within their first month, and 14.48% within their first six months In this article, we will define voluntary vs. involuntary turnover briefly. Then we’ll dig deeper into the voluntary employee turnover types and how they impact your business. Voluntary vs. Involuntary Turnover Involuntary employee turnover happens when employees are terminated from their positions. Voluntary employee turnover happens when employees willingly choose to lea
[5]: ve their positions. Let’s focus on some of the most common categories of voluntary turnover: - Job Abandonment: This happens when an employee doesn’t call or show up to work for a set period of time. They’ve abandoned their post. - Another Job: This is when an employee finds employment at a different company. Typically, we see the reason for this move is money-related or bad management-motivated. If your organization is typical, this category is probably the most significant percentage of your voluntary turnover. Sound risk mitigation for this type of turnover is determining if you are paying your employees enough for your industry, job role, and region. Or, you may need to research and investigate your managers to see if there are personality clashes, leadership conflicts, or other issues that need to be remedied. - Personal Reasons: This could include health reasons, handling family issues, and even a change in priorities in their personal life, such as returning to school, relocating to another state, or wanting a change in industry. - Job Dissatisfaction: An employee leaves because they are not satisfied with their position or the organization. Out of these four reasons, this i
[5]: s something your organization probably has the most control of. By finding out the causes of your workforce’s dissatisfaction – through surveys, discussions, coaching – you can start making positive changes in the work environment fairly quickly. A Work Institute report from 2020 shows 20% of employees leave their jobs due to frustration over a lack of growth, job advancement, and development opportunities. Using your HR data and analytics to drill down to the real reasons your employees leave will help inform and direct your employee retention and career growth strategies. And a reduction in employee turnover will have a positive effect on your organization’s bottom line! The Costs of Voluntary Turnover Business leaders must realize the cost of replacing employees is not merely the price of advertisements or headhunter fees. Filling vacant positions, onboarding, training, and lost productivity are expensive costs for organizations, especially when employees that leave have in-demand, specialized skills or valuable institutional knowledge and intellectual assets. So let’s also consider these factors that are included in the costs: - Paying other employees overtime to handle the rol
[5]: e while it’s unfilled - Decreased productivity due to loss of workgroup synergy - Decrease in morale, engagement, and satisfaction by the team - Hiring temporary help while recruiting a replacement - Conducting exit interviews - Recruiting costs - Onboarding - Training It’s been estimated that each employee that leaves costs their employer about 33% of their annual earnings. Your involuntary turnover rate is 7/100 or 7%. When you add 5% and 7
[5]: % together, you have an annual turnover rate of 12%. Reducing the employee turnover rate is one of the crucial tasks of team leaders. Why? Because a high turnover rate implies that the organization is incurring high costs of operations due to recruiting new employees, the costs of training and development, the loss of productivity, and possibly even the loss of business. [5]: right fit, there or more chances that the employee will be satisfied with that job. - Retain Key Employees: Concentrate on retaining key employees because as stated above, costs begin to add up when employees leave. When you retain your most experienced, seasoned, and talented employees, you help ensure your company’s strength. And guess what? Employee retention is not just the function of the HR department. Employee retention is everyone’s responsibility through employee recognition, regular performance feedback, fair rewards according to employees’ contributions, and even increasing employee retention with HR data. - Create Positive Relationships: Good, open, and honest two-way communication between managers and employees not only reduces problems but builds trust in relationships. The sources define voluntary and involuntary turnover as two distinct categories, but only one of them, source [4], treats involuntary termination as a phenomenon worth its own cost analysis, and even that source stops short of putting a dollar figure on it. The cost studies you'd cite for a "cost of a bad hire" section largely present a single blended replacement-cost figure and don't split it by exit type.

**How the sources define the split.** Voluntary turnover is employee-initiated: resigning for a better offer, dissatisfaction with pay or management, personal circumstances, or lack of growth [1][2][3][5]. Involuntary turnover is employer-initiated, most often tied to poor performance, policy violations, or restructuring [1][2][3]. Source [4] refines involuntary termination further into "with cause" (fired for a specific reason, usually after warnings or a performance improvement plan) and "without cause" (layoffs driven by financial or strategic conditions rather than the employee's conduct). Source [5] adds a practical wrinkle: some voluntary departures, like job abandonment (an employee simply stops showing up), sit closer to the line between the two categories than a clean either/or split suggests.

**Where the cost figures come from, and why they don't separate by exit type.** The headline numbers you'd use in a "real cost" section, SHRM's 50%-200% of annual salary [1][3][5], Josh Bersin's 1.5-2x salary estimate [1][3], the Work Institute's 25%-200% range [2], and the $617 billion 2018 national estimate for voluntary turnover specifically [5], are calculated the same way regardless of why the seat emptied: recruitment cost, onboarding and training cost (source [3] cites $874 per employee in 2024), the productivity ramp-up period, and lost institutional knowledge [1][2][3]. None of the gathered sources runs a controlled comparison showing that a termination costs meaningfully more or less to replace than a resignation for the same role. Source [5] does isolate voluntary turnover's cost at roughly 33% of the departing employee's annual earnings, but it doesn't provide a matching involuntary-only figure to compare it against, so a like-for-like comparison isn't available in this material.

**Where the two paths do seem to diverge, based on what's here.** The clearest distinction in the sources isn't voluntary-versus-involuntary at all, it's functional-versus-dysfunctional turnover [1]. A departure is "functional" when a low performer leaves and room opens for a stronger hire; it's "dysfunctional" when a high performer leaves and the organization is worse off. That axis cuts across both exit types: a voluntary resignation by a strong performer is dysfunctional and costly, while an involuntary termination of a weak performer is functional and can even be a net positive. So the cost profile appears to track performance and role criticality more than it tracks who initiated the exit.

Beyond that, source [4] flags a few process differences specific to involuntary exits rather than cost differences: heightened legal exposure, stricter offboarding requirements (revoking system access, securing termination documentation), and the fact that "without cause" layoffs are strategic decisions rather than signals of a hiring or management problem, whereas "with cause" firings can indicate a flawed hiring process in the first place. Source [3] notes reputational and morale effects tied to *how* a departure is communicated and handled internally, and source [1] notes that dysfunctional turnover specifically harms operations, but neither source quantifies whether an involuntary exit compounds morale damage more or less than a voluntary one; the morale and culture costs described (co-workers questioning why someone left, remaining staff absorbing extra workload, disengagement) are described as effects of turnover broadly, not scaled differently by exit type [1][2][3].

**Bottom line.** Based on the gathered material, I cannot confirm that the research shows meaningfully different cost profiles for voluntary versus involuntary bad-hire exits. The available cost studies (SHRM, Bersin, Work Institute) report replacement cost as a function of salary and role level, not exit type, and the one source that treats involuntary termination as its own topic [4] focuses on legal, procedural, and offboarding differences rather than a distinct dollar figure. The dimension the sources actually tie to compounding organizational cost is functional versus dysfunctional turnover, that is, whether the person who left was a low performer or a high performer, which can apply to either a voluntary or an involuntary departure.

1. Talent Acquisition Cost Analyst: Focuses on the direct, measurable spend of hiring — job board and advertising fees, recruiter and agency commissions, executive search retainers, referral bonuses, and cost-per-hire benchmarks — and how these vary by role level and industry.
2. HR Operations and Process Specialist: Focuses on the indirect cost of time — time-to-fill and time-to-hire metrics, the productivity drag of unfilled positions, interviewer and hiring-manager hours spent screening and interviewing, and how process inefficiency (multi-tier recruitment models, redundant screening steps) compounds cost.
3. Employee Turnover and Retention Economist: Focuses on the downstream cost of a bad or short-lived hire — replacement cost calculations, lost productivity during ramp-up, the compounding effect of voluntary versus involuntary turnover, and how poor recruitment decisions feed directly into turnover statistics.
4. Recruitment Technology and Systems Editor: Focuses on the cost of the tooling layer — applicant tracking system licensing, HR information system integration, e-recruiting platform subscriptions, and the trade-off between automation investment and manual labor savings.
5. Risk, Compliance, and Screening Specialist: Focuses on the cost of due diligence and legal exposure — background check and identity verification fees, safer-recruitment and disability-accommodation compliance, and the financial risk of illegal practices or negligent-hiring claims.
6. Candidate Experience and Employer Brand Advocate: Focuses on the often-uncounted cost of a poor candidate journey — onboarding investment, the reputational cost of a broken job-hunting experience on the applicant side, and how weak employer branding raises sourcing and referral costs over time.
7. Cost–Benefit Methodology Editor: Focuses on how to actually measure and frame "the real cost" rigorously — discounting future costs (like turnover-driven replacement), separating direct from opportunity costs, and applying cost-benefit analysis principles so the article's cost claims are structured and comparable rather than anecdotal.

Topic you want to write: The Real Cost of Recruitment in

Your persona besides being a Wikipedia writer: Basic fact writer: Basic fact writer focusing on broadly covering the basic facts about the topic.

Conversation history:
You: How is "the cost of recruitment" typically defined and measured, and what are the main categories of expenses it includes (e.g., advertising, agency fees, staff time, onboarding, lost productivity)?
Expert: The cost of recruitment, most often tracked as "cost per hire" (CPH), is the total amount an organization spends to identify, attract, and select a candidate to fill a job vacancy . It is calculated with a standard formula: total recruiting costs (internal plus external) divided by the number of hires made in a given period . The Society for Human Resource Management (SHRM) treats this as the industry-standard formula, and its 2025 benchmarking survey of 2,371 members put the average cost per hire at $5,475 for nonexecutive roles and $35,879 for executive roles, with executive hires running nearly seven times more expensive than nonexecutive ones . Earlier SHRM data cited an average of roughly $4,700 per hire, though many practitioners estimate that when every cost is accounted for, a hire can total three to four times the position's salary .
Because a "hire" can be defined narrowly or broadly, organizations first decide who counts: some include internal transfers, temporary staff, freelancers, and fixed-term contract workers, while others exclude employees gained through mergers or acquisitions or those on a third-party payroll . The time period matters too. Cost per hire can be tracked monthly, quarterly, or annually, and can be broken down further by department or role, since a specialized or executive search naturally costs far more than a high-volume frontline hire .
**Categories of expense**
Most sources split recruitment costs into two broad buckets, often labeled "internal vs. external" or "direct vs. indirect."
*Internal (time-based) costs* cover the labor spent running the hiring process itself: recruiter and in-house recruitment team salaries and benefits, the allocated share of a hiring manager's time spent interviewing (managers reportedly spend only about 13% of their total time on hiring and onboarding tasks, but that slice still carries a cost), HR coordination time, and prorated fees for an applicant tracking system (ATS) or other recruiting software . Administrative overhead such as office space, equipment, and compliance-related document processing also falls here .
*External (invoice-based) costs* are third-party expenses that can be summed directly from accounts payable: job board and career-site advertising, social media and print advertising, recruitment or executive search agency commissions (commonly 15-25% of a hire's first-year salary), employee referral bonuses (typically $500-$5,000 per successful hire), background and drug checks, pre-employment assessments and psychometric testing, candidate travel and interview-related accommodation, career-fair participation fees, relocation expenses, and signing bonuses .
Beyond these two hard-cost buckets, several sources emphasize a category of "soft" or indirect costs that are harder to quantify but still real. One SHRM-sourced estimate splits total recruiting spend as roughly 30-40% hard costs and 60% soft costs, the latter being the time department leaders and managers divert from their normal work to screen applications, sit in interview rounds, and make hiring decisions . Soft costs also include lost productivity: the output gap left by an unfilled position, the "unmoored" disruption a team feels when it loses a member who connected different work groups, and the emotional and mental toll on hiring teams dealing with candidate ghosting and rising demands . Losing a strong candidate mid-process to a faster-moving competitor, and the cost of a declined offer after a candidate has already accepted (backing out affected roughly 35% of accepted offers in early 2025, by one account), represent pure sunk cost, since the full recruiting spend is incurred with no hire to show for it .
Cost per hire explicitly stops at the point of hire. It does not include post-hire training beyond initial onboarding, productivity ramp-up time, or ongoing employment costs; those are tracked under separate metrics such as cost of vacancy or cost per employee . Analysts also caution against reading cost per hire in isolation: a lower number can reflect efficiency, or it can mask under-investment in employer branding and quality of hire, or hidden, uncaptured hiring-manager time, so many organizations pair it with quality-of-hire or 90-day retention measures for a fuller picture .

Conversation history:
You: When organizations calculate "cost-per-hire," what are the standard cost categories included in that figure, and are there recognized industry benchmarks (like those from SHRM or similar bodies) that define what counts as "direct" versus "indirect" recruitment costs?
Expert: The standard, industry-recognized metric for this is Cost-Per-Hire (CPH), and it does have a formal specification, not just an ad-hoc convention. In 2012 the Society for Human Resource Management (SHRM) and the American National Standards Institute (ANSI) jointly formalized a CPH formula as ANSI/SHRM 06001.2012, giving the field a shared methodology for comparing hiring costs across organizations . That standard remains the reference point cited by virtually every source on this topic, even when they disagree on details .
**The core formula**
The SHRM/ANSI standard defines cost-per-hire simply as the mean average of total recruiting costs divided by the number of hires in a period :
Cost Per Hire = (Total Internal Recruiting Costs + Total External Recruiting Costs) ÷ Total Number of Hires
The official standard organizes costs along an internal/external axis, not a direct/indirect one, though several sources use "direct" and "indirect" as rough synonyms for that split, and SHRM's own Human Capital Benchmarking material describes the total as covering "internal and external, direct and indirect costs" together, suggesting the two framings overlap rather than sitting cleanly apart .
**Internal (or "direct/hard") costs**
These are costs generated within the organization. Sources consistently list:
- Recruiter salaries, benefits, and bonuses, generally allocated by the percentage of time spent on recruiting
- Hiring manager and interviewer time, calculated as hourly rate times hours spent, though this is sometimes flagged as optional because it's hard to track
- HR/administrative coordination time and recruiting department overhead, including a prorated share of office costs and compliance work
- ATS (applicant tracking system) and other recruiting software subscriptions, prorated across hires
- Employee referral program payouts
- Recruiter training and development
**External (or "direct/hard") costs**
These are amounts paid to outside vendors and are more straightforward to sum from invoices:
- Job board and advertising fees, roughly $50–$1,500 per posting depending on the source
- Recruitment agency or headhunter fees, commonly 15–25% of first-year salary for contingency search and up to 40% for retained executive search
- Background checks, drug screening, and pre-employment assessments
- Candidate travel, relocation, and signing bonuses

Topic you want to write: The Real Cost of Recruitment in

Your persona besides being a Wikipedia writer: HR Operations and Process Specialist: Focuses on the indirect cost of time — time-to-fill and time-to-hire metrics, the productivity drag of unfilled positions, interviewer and hiring-manager hours spent screening and interviewing, and how process inefficiency (multi-tier recruitment models, redundant screening steps) compounds cost.

Conversation history:
You: How do organizations typically calculate the actual dollar cost of a position remaining vacant for each additional day, and what factors (lost output, overtime for existing staff, delayed revenue) are usually included in that calculation?
Expert: Organizations calculate the cost of a vacant position by first establishing a daily dollar value for the role, then multiplying that daily figure by the number of days the position stays open. Several named methodologies converge on this same basic structure, though the inputs they use to build the "daily value" figure differ.
## The core formula
The most common version starts with the position's value to the business and subtracts what the company is saving by not paying the departed employee's salary, then adds back whatever it costs to cover the work in the meantime. One recruitment guide states it as: daily cost of vacancy equals (annual value the role generates ÷ 260 working days) minus (annual salary ÷ 260) plus daily interim-cover cost, with the total then multiplied by the number of working days the role stays open . Applied to a sales role generating €300,000 a year on a €60,000 salary, with a manager spending €150 a day covering the gap, that works out to roughly €1,073 a day, or about €47,000 across a 44-day vacancy .
A related version published by Indeed/Addison Group-style sources and DISHER Talent Solutions calculates a daily revenue-per-employee figure (company annual revenue divided by headcount, divided by roughly 260 working days), adjusts it by a job-level multiplier (low = 1, mid = 2, senior = 3), and multiplies that adjusted daily figure by the number of vacancy days. A $5 million company with 50 employees and a mid-level role vacant for 60 days works out to $46,080 .
A third version, laid out step by step by an SHRM-sourced source, works from the position's own salary rather than company-wide revenue per employee. It (1) determines the annual salary, (2) divides by roughly 260 working days to get a daily cost, (3) estimates the expected number of vacant days from historical or industry data, (4) multiplies the daily cost by that number of days, (5) adds 31% (the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics estimate for benefits) to the daily cost to get payroll-plus-benefits savings, and (6) nets that savings figure against lost revenue and coverage costs to arrive at the final cost of vacancy. For a $75,000 nurse role vacant 60 days, requiring a $36,000 traveling-nurse fill-in on top of $4,000 in hiring costs, the net cost of vacancy came to $17,327.20 after subtracting $22,672.80 in payroll and benefits savings . For a $60,000 sales role generating $500,000 in annual revenue, vacant 60 days, the same method (starting from lost revenue rather than salary) produced a cost of vacancy of $98,615.62 .
A three-tier framework separates the calculation into direct financial costs (revenue impact, coverage costs, recruitment and onboarding expenses), operational impact costs (team productivity loss, quality and service degradation, strategic opportunity cost), and cultural and retention costs (burnout, employer brand erosion, manager productivity loss). Its simplified formula sums daily revenue impact, daily coverage costs, and daily team productivity loss, multiplies by days vacant, then adds recruitment costs. A mid-level marketing manager position, vacant 90 days with $400 in daily revenue impact, $300 in daily coverage costs, $600 in daily productivity loss, and $8,000 in recruitment costs, totals $125,000 .
## Factors typically included
**Lost output or revenue.** For revenue-generating roles (sales, billable consulting, production), organizations calculate average revenue per employee per day and multiply by days vacant . For non-revenue roles, a defensible proxy is company-wide revenue per employee, since not having any employee in the seat still means zero output from that seat . One writer describes several simplified variants of this same idea: average revenue per lost employee, a salary multiplier of lost revenue (based on research suggesting an employee's value runs one to three times their salary), and a straight "revenue lost" calculation for revenue-generating jobs .
**Overtime and coverage costs for existing staff.** Nearly every source lists this as a direct cost: paying existing employees overtime, often at 1.5 times the regular rate, or hiring temporary workers and contractors, who typically cost 40 to 80% more than a full-time employee . One worked example shows two engineers working 20 extra overtime hours a week each at $75 an hour, adding $6,000 in labor costs in a single month .
**Payroll and benefits savings (netted against the above).** Because the company is not paying the vacant position's salary and benefits during the gap, several formulas subtract this savings from the total. Benefits are commonly estimated at 31% of salary, per Bureau of Labor Statistics data .
**Delayed revenue and strategic opportunity cost.** This covers stalled product launches, missed market windows, and postponed strategic initiatives that depend on the vacant role, described as "the most overlooked category" in the three-tier framework, and echoed by a source noting that delayed initiatives compound losses well beyond a single salary .
**Recruitment and hiring costs.** Job board and advertising spend, recruiter and HR hours, and higher offer amounts needed to close candidates in a prolonged search. Industry cost-per-hire figures cited range from about $4,000 up to $20,000 depending on role level, with SHRM separately citing an average cost-per-hire near $4,700 .
**Productivity loss across the remaining team.** Estimated as (number of affected team members × percentage productivity loss × average fully-loaded cost per employee × days vacant), with context-switching and task fragmentation reducing overall team productivity by an estimated 20 to 40% .
**Quality, customer service, and morale effects.** These are the costs most sources describe as "hidden" or "soft" and harder to quantify precisely, including decreased customer satisfaction, higher defect or error rates, team burnout, and increased turnover risk. Gallup research is cited for the finding that overtime-driven burnout can cut productivity by up to 68% and that burned-out employees are 2.6 times more likely to leave . A widely cited American Express survey found that 33% of customers consider switching providers after just one poor service experience, and Forrester Research estimated that a 1-point improvement in customer satisfaction can translate to roughly $1 billion in revenue for a typical Fortune 1000 company .
## Reported dollar figures and time-to-fill benchmarks
Reported ranges vary widely by source and role type. SHRM data puts average monthly vacancy costs between $4,129 and $5,733 , while a separate estimate citing Lightcast Research puts the figure closer to $25,000 per month . One source describes daily costs in key roles ranging from $7,000 to $12,000, with one documented case reaching $200,000 per day . Average time-to-fill is reported at 43 to 44 days in the U.S., up from 29 days in 2010 .
## What the calculations typically exclude
Several sources note explicitly that even the more detailed formulas leave out harder-to-quantify indirect costs, including reduced team morale, increased workload stress on remaining employees, lost business opportunities, and the cascading effect where one vacancy-driven burnout episode triggers further turnover . One source distinguishes cost of vacancy (lost output while a role sits empty, accruing daily) from cost-per-hire (money spent once, at the point of hire) and cost of a bad hire (ongoing loss from the wrong person in the role after hiring), noting that organizations that cut cost-per-hire by reducing sourcing budgets can inadvertently raise their cost of vacancy by leaving roles open longer .

You: How is "the cost of recruitment" typically defined and measured, and what are the main categories of expenses it includes (e.g., advertising, agency fees, staff time, onboarding, lost productivity)?
Expert: The cost of recruitment, most often tracked as "cost per hire" (CPH), is the total amount an organization spends to identify, attract, and select a candidate to fill a job vacancy . It is calculated with a standard formula: total recruiting costs (internal plus external) divided by the number of hires made in a given period . The Society for Human Resource Management (SHRM) treats this as the industry-standard formula, and its 2025 benchmarking survey of 2,371 members put the average cost per hire at $5,475 for nonexecutive roles and $35,879 for executive roles, with executive hires running nearly seven times more expensive than nonexecutive ones . Earlier SHRM data cited an average of roughly $4,700 per hire, though many practitioners estimate that when every cost is accounted for, a hire can total three to four times the position's salary .
Because a "hire" can be defined narrowly or broadly, organizations first decide who counts: some include internal transfers, temporary staff, freelancers, and fixed-term contract workers, while others exclude employees gained through mergers or acquisitions or those on a third-party payroll . The time period matters too. Cost per hire can be tracked monthly, quarterly, or annually, and can be broken down further by department or role, since a specialized or executive search naturally costs far more than a high-volume frontline hire .
**Categories of expense**
Most sources split recruitment costs into two broad buckets, often labeled "internal vs. external" or "direct vs. indirect."
*Internal (time-based) costs* cover the labor spent running the hiring process itself: recruiter and in-house recruitment team salaries and benefits, the allocated share of a hiring manager's time spent interviewing (managers reportedly spend only about 13% of their total time on hiring and onboarding tasks, but that slice still carries a cost), HR coordination time, and prorated fees for an applicant tracking system (ATS) or other recruiting software . Administrative overhead such as office space, equipment, and compliance-related document processing also falls here .
*External (invoice-based) costs* are third-party expenses that can be summed directly from accounts payable: job board and career-site advertising, social media and print advertising, recruitment or executive search agency commissions (commonly 15-25% of a hire's first-year salary), employee referral bonuses (typically $500-$5,000 per successful hire), background and drug checks, pre-employment assessments and psychometric testing, candidate travel and interview-related accommodation, career-fair participation fees, relocation expenses, and signing bonuses .
Beyond these two hard-cost buckets, several sources emphasize a category of "soft" or indirect costs that are harder to quantify but still real. One SHRM-sourced estimate splits total recruiting spend as roughly 30-40% hard costs and 60% soft costs, the latter being the time department leaders and managers divert from their normal work to screen applications, sit in interview rounds, and make hiring decisions . Soft costs also include lost productivity: the output gap left by an unfilled position, the "unmoored" disruption a team feels when it loses a member who connected different work groups, and the emotional and mental toll on hiring teams dealing with candidate ghosting and rising demands . Losing a strong candidate mid-process to a faster-moving competitor, and the cost of a declined offer after a candidate has already accepted (backing out affected roughly 35% of accepted offers in early 2025, by one account), represent pure sunk cost, since the full recruiting spend is incurred with no hire to show for it .
Cost per hire explicitly stops at the point of hire. It does not include post-hire training beyond initial onboarding, productivity ramp-up time, or ongoing employment costs; those are tracked under separate metrics such as cost of vacancy or cost per employee . Analysts also caution against reading cost per hire in isolation: a lower number can reflect efficiency, or it can mask under-investment in employer branding and quality of hire, or hidden, uncaptured hiring-manager time, so many organizations pair it with quality-of-hire or 90-day retention measures for a fuller picture .
You: How does cost per hire vary by industry, company size, and geographic region, and are there notable historical trends showing whether recruitment costs have been rising or falling over time?
Expert: Cost per hire varies substantially along several dimensions, though the available data is concentrated on the United States and offers little direct geographic comparison.
**By industry.** SHRM Benchmarking Services data shows average cost per hire ranging from about $1,070 to over $6,000 depending on sector. Accommodation, food service, arts, entertainment, and recreation sit at the low end ($1,070), while professional, scientific, and technical services along with communication sit at the high end ($6,464). In between: manufacturing ($3,497), public administration/education ($4,160), information/finance/insurance/real estate ($4,173), construction/utilities/agriculture/mining ($4,371), wholesale/retail trade/transportation/warehousing ($4,705), healthcare and social services ($4,770), and administrative support/other services ($6,338) . A separate analysis citing TimeClick data frames the spread differently by named industry: retail/hospitality at $2,700, technology at $6,200-$8,000, healthcare at $9,000-$12,000, skilled trades above $12,000, and legal/professional services at $16,000-$20,000. That source attributes healthcare's elevated cost to credential verification, licensing requirements, and an ongoing talent shortage, putting healthcare hiring at two to three times the national average .
**By company size.** Small businesses generally face lower total dollar costs per hire but a different cost structure than larger organizations. One SMB-focused breakdown puts direct cost per hire at $500-$1,500 for a company's first hires (1-5 employees), rising to $1,500-$4,000 direct cost at 25-50 employees, versus the SHRM all-size benchmark of roughly $4,700; when indirect costs (founder or manager time, vacancy cost) are added, the SMB total runs $2,500-$10,000 depending on size . The gap is attributed to three factors: small businesses typically don't pay for an applicant tracking system, rarely use agencies for standard roles, and carry no dedicated recruiting staff overhead — costs that enterprise companies absorb into their per-hire figure . A separate analysis notes that smaller companies often face higher per-hire costs despite lower total spending, because they lack scale to spread fixed costs (recruiter salaries, ATS licenses, employer branding) across many hires the way an enterprise spreading $2 million across 20 recruiters making 1,000 hires can . Consistent with this, cost per hire is the top-tracked HR metric for 47% of businesses with 5-19 employees and 54% of businesses with 20-49 employees, according to a Paychex survey, reflecting how much weight each individual hire carries at that scale .
**By role/seniority**, which compounds both industry and size effects: entry-level hires run $2,000-$3,000, mid-level professional $4,000-$6,000, technical/engineering $6,200-$8,000, senior/director $10,000-$20,000, and executive/C-suite $28,000-$35,879 — roughly a 12-times gap between entry-level and executive hiring, per data compiled from SHRM and ScoutLogic .
**By geographic region**, the gathered sources do not provide a breakdown; all cited benchmarks (SHRM, CareerBuilder, DOL, Paychex, Gem, Employ) are reported at the US national level without regional or international disaggregation. I cannot answer the regional-variation part of the question based on the available information.
**Historical trend: rising, not falling.** Multiple sources point the same direction. SHRM's often-cited $4,700 average cost per hire traces to its 2016 Human Capital Benchmarking Report; by 2024 that figure was reported to have risen about 14% from pre-pandemic levels . SHRM's 2025 Benchmarking Report puts the current non-executive average at $5,475, describing the older $4,700 figure as outdated and reflecting "a prior SHRM benchmarking cycle" . Executive cost per hire has climbed faster: from $28,329 in earlier reporting to $35,879 in the 2025 report, a 21% increase from 2022 alone and a 113% increase from 2017 . Separately, Appcast's Recruitment Marketing Benchmark Report found that both cost-per-application and cost-per-hire rose sharply in 2025 despite a softer labor market, attributed to shifts in job board pricing and programmatic ad models — in other words, hiring costs have kept climbing even when hiring demand cooled . One partial counter-trend: Employ's 2026 Recruiting Benchmarks Report found median time-to-fill dropped from 67.7 days in 2025 to 63.5 days in 2026, which would modestly reduce vacancy-cost exposure even as headline cost-per-hire figures continue rising .
Taken together, the pattern across all these sources is consistent: average cost per hire has been on an upward trajectory for at least a decade, the executive/non-executive gap is widening faster than the overall average, and the industry, size, and role variation is large enough that any single national average, whether $4,700 or $5,475, masks a real range of roughly $1,000 to well over $35,000 depending on which of those variables applies .

Because a "hire" can be defined narrowly or broadly, organizations first decide who counts: some include internal transfers, temporary staff, freelancers, and fixed-term contract workers, while others exclude employees gained through mergers or acquisitions or those on a third-party payroll . The time period matters too. Cost per hire can be tracked monthly, quarterly, or annually, and can be broken down further by department or role, since a specialized or executive search naturally costs far more than a high-volume frontline hire .
**Categories of expense**
Most sources split recruitment costs into two broad buckets, often labeled "internal vs. external" or "direct vs. indirect."
*Internal (time-based) costs* cover the labor spent running the hiring process itself: recruiter and in-house recruitment team salaries and benefits, the allocated share of a hiring manager's time spent interviewing (managers reportedly spend only about 13% of their total time on hiring and onboarding tasks, but that slice still carries a cost), HR coordination time, and prorated fees for an applicant tracking system (ATS) or other recruiting software . Administrative overhead such as office space, equipment, and compliance-related document processing also falls here .
*External (invoice-based) costs* are third-party expenses that can be summed directly from accounts payable: job board and career-site advertising, social media and print advertising, recruitment or executive search agency commissions (commonly 15-25% of a hire's first-year salary), employee referral bonuses (typically $500-$5,000 per successful hire), background and drug checks, pre-employment assessments and psychometric testing, candidate travel and interview-related accommodation, career-fair participation fees, relocation expenses, and signing bonuses .
Beyond these two hard-cost buckets, several sources emphasize a category of "soft" or indirect costs that are harder to quantify but still real. One SHRM-sourced estimate splits total recruiting spend as roughly 30-40% hard costs and 60% soft costs, the latter being the time department leaders and managers divert from their normal work to screen applications, sit in interview rounds, and make hiring decisions . Soft costs also include lost productivity: the output gap left by an unfilled position, the "unmoored" disruption a team feels when it loses a member who connected different work groups, and the emotional and mental toll on hiring teams dealing with candidate ghosting and rising demands . Losing a strong candidate mid-process to a faster-moving competitor, and the cost of a declined offer after a candidate has already accepted (backing out affected roughly 35% of accepted offers in early 2025, by one account), represent pure sunk cost, since the full recruiting spend is incurred with no hire to show for it .
Cost per hire explicitly stops at the point of hire. It does not include post-hire training beyond initial onboarding, productivity ramp-up time, or ongoing employment costs; those are tracked under separate metrics such as cost of vacancy or cost per employee . Analysts also caution against reading cost per hire in isolation: a lower number can reflect efficiency, or it can mask under-investment in employer branding and quality of hire, or hidden, uncaptured hiring-manager time, so many organizations pair it with quality-of-hire or 90-day retention measures for a fuller picture .
You: How does cost per hire vary by industry, company size, and geographic region, and are there notable historical trends showing whether recruitment costs have been rising or falling over time?
Expert: Cost per hire varies substantially along several dimensions, though the available data is concentrated on the United States and offers little direct geographic comparison.
**By industry.** SHRM Benchmarking Services data shows average cost per hire ranging from about $1,070 to over $6,000 depending on sector. Accommodation, food service, arts, entertainment, and recreation sit at the low end ($1,070), while professional, scientific, and technical services along with communication sit at the high end ($6,464). In between: manufacturing ($3,497), public administration/education ($4,160), information/finance/insurance/real estate ($4,173), construction/utilities/agriculture/mining ($4,371), wholesale/retail trade/transportation/warehousing ($4,705), healthcare and social services ($4,770), and administrative support/other services ($6,338) . A separate analysis citing TimeClick data frames the spread differently by named industry: retail/hospitality at $2,700, technology at $6,200-$8,000, healthcare at $9,000-$12,000, skilled trades above $12,000, and legal/professional services at $16,000-$20,000. That source attributes healthcare's elevated cost to credential verification, licensing requirements, and an ongoing talent shortage, putting healthcare hiring at two to three times the national average .
**By company size.** Small businesses generally face lower total dollar costs per hire but a different cost structure than larger organizations. One SMB-focused breakdown puts direct cost per hire at $500-$1,500 for a company's first hires (1-5 employees), rising to $1,500-$4,000 direct cost at 25-50 employees, versus the SHRM all-size benchmark of roughly $4,700; when indirect costs (founder or manager time, vacancy cost) are added, the SMB total runs $2,500-$10,000 depending on size . The gap is attributed to three factors: small businesses typically don't pay for an applicant tracking system, rarely use agencies for standard roles, and carry no dedicated recruiting staff overhead — costs that enterprise companies absorb into their per-hire figure . A separate analysis notes that smaller companies often face higher per-hire costs despite lower total spending, because they lack scale to spread fixed costs (recruiter salaries, ATS licenses, employer branding) across many hires the way an enterprise spreading $2 million across 20 recruiters making 1,000 hires can . Consistent with this, cost per hire is the top-tracked HR metric for 47% of businesses with 5-19 employees and 54% of businesses with 20-49 employees, according to a Paychex survey, reflecting how much weight each individual hire carries at that scale .
**By role/seniority**, which compounds both industry and size effects: entry-level hires run $2,000-$3,000, mid-level professional $4,000-$6,000, technical/engineering $6,200-$8,000, senior/director $10,000-$20,000, and executive/C-suite $28,000-$35,879 — roughly a 12-times gap between entry-level and executive hiring, per data compiled from SHRM and ScoutLogic .
**By geographic region**, the gathered sources do not provide a breakdown; all cited benchmarks (SHRM, CareerBuilder, DOL, Paychex, Gem, Employ) are reported at the US national level without regional or international disaggregation. I cannot answer the regional-variation part of the question based on the available information.
**Historical trend: rising, not falling.** Multiple sources point the same direction. SHRM's often-cited $4,700 average cost per hire traces to its 2016 Human Capital Benchmarking Report; by 2024 that figure was reported to have risen about 14% from pre-pandemic levels . SHRM's 2025 Benchmarking Report puts the current non-executive average at $5,475, describing the older $4,700 figure as outdated and reflecting "a prior SHRM benchmarking cycle" . Executive cost per hire has climbed faster: from $28,329 in earlier reporting to $35,879 in the 2025 report, a 21% increase from 2022 alone and a 113% increase from 2017 . Separately, Appcast's Recruitment Marketing Benchmark Report found that both cost-per-application and cost-per-hire rose sharply in 2025 despite a softer labor market, attributed to shifts in job board pricing and programmatic ad models — in other words, hiring costs have kept climbing even when hiring demand cooled . One partial counter-trend: Employ's 2026 Recruiting Benchmarks Report found median time-to-fill dropped from 67.7 days in 2025 to 63.5 days in 2026, which would modestly reduce vacancy-cost exposure even as headline cost-per-hire figures continue rising .
